column5: God reverses poor and rich
column6: The commentary places noble and lowest ranks inside one human loss; Hannah's song says YHWH makes poor and rich and brings low and high down or up, making rank reversible under divine sovereignty.

column5: poor raised to sit with princes
column6: The commentary names the lowest social ranks; Hannah's song says God raises the poor from dust and seats the needy with princes, directly overturning the status scale used by Noah's accusers.

column5: poor lifted from dust in Hallel
column6: The commentary recalls the lowest freedmen; this Hallel praise celebrates YHWH lifting the poor from dust and the needy from the ash heap, turning rank reversal into communal liturgy.

column5: needy seated with princes
column6: The next verse says the needy are seated with princes; it gives the commentary's high/low contrast a liturgical image of the low receiving the highest social seat.

column5: equal half-shekel for rich and poor
column6: The census ransom is one half-shekel per person: the rich may not give more and the poor less. This Torah rule gives the commentary's inclusion of high and low a concrete equal measure.

column5: no boasting in wisdom, might, or wealth
column6: The commentary treats lineage and rank as human status measures; Jeremiah forbids boasting in wisdom, strength, or riches, showing that several forms of social capital cannot secure standing.

column5: boast in knowing the God who does justice
column6: Jeremiah redirects boasting to understanding and knowing YHWH, who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness; this specifies the commentary's shift from lineage to religious and ethical standing.

column5: haughty removed from God's mountain
column6: The commentary says high rank cannot exempt anyone from loss; Zephaniah says God will remove the haughty from the holy mountain on the day of judgment, directly lowering status before God.

column5: humble remnant seeks refuge in YHWH
column6: The commentary makes the distinction by faith and deeds; Zephaniah leaves a humble, lowly people who seek refuge in YHWH's name, joining low status to trust rather than pedigree.

column5: wild branches share the cultivated root
column6: The commentary calls the root an image of lineage; Paul pictures Gentile believers grafted into Israel's olive tree to share its root, giving the lineage image a specific scene of inclusion across peoples.

column5: root supports branches, so do not boast
column6: The commentary describes people grounding superiority in lineage; Paul tells the grafted branch not to boast over natural branches because the root supports it, explicitly overturning pedigree pride.

column5: standing by faith, not inherited branch status
column6: The commentary says distinction turns on faith rather than lineage; Paul says natural branches were broken off through unbelief while Gentile branches stand through faith, then warns against pride.

column5: descent from Israel is not sufficient
column6: The commentary denies that lineage determines the human verdict; Paul says not all descended from Israel belong to Israel, distinguishing physical descent from covenant standing.

column5: children of promise, not flesh alone
column6: Paul explains that children of the flesh are not thereby God's children and that children of promise count as offspring; this gives the commentary's lineage/status issue a specific theological redefinition.

column5: outward identity does not decide standing
column6: The commentary says inherited rank is not the criterion; Paul says Jewish identity and circumcision are not merely outward or bodily, challenging status carried by visible ancestry markers.

column5: inward identity and praise from God
column6: Paul defines the true identity by circumcision of the heart through the Spirit and praise from God, giving the commentary's move from lineage to inward religious standing a specific formulation.

column5: believers become children of God
column6: The commentary says lineage does not decide who belongs among the saved; John says those who receive and believe in Jesus' name are given the status of God's children.

column5: birth not from blood but from God
column6: John specifies that God's children are not born from blood or human will but from God, directly denying natural descent as the source of religious standing.

column5: outcasts enter before religious leaders
column6: In Jesus' temple dispute, he says tax collectors and prostitutes are entering God's kingdom ahead of the leaders; this closely matches the commentary's picture of elites discrediting a prophet because low-status people follow him.

column5: belief and repentance distinguish the groups
column6: Jesus explains that the outcasts believed John while the leaders did not repent after seeing it; this makes response to the message, not public rank, the reason for their different standing.

column5: tax collector justified over Pharisee
column6: In the paired prayer scene, Jesus says the tax collector goes home justified rather than the Pharisee; the religiously prestigious figure does not outrank the despised man who humbles himself before God.

column5: greatness defined as service
column6: The commentary names inherited and social rank, then says deeds mark distinction; Jesus says the one who wants to be great must become a servant, replacing status with conduct.

column5: first place defined as slavery to all
column6: Jesus continues that the one who wants to be first must become a slave to all, directly reversing the rank logic behind the commentary's noble and lowest social categories.

column5: weaker parts are indispensable
column6: The commentary notes that low and weak people remain within the human category; Paul says body parts that seem weaker are indispensable, giving low status a necessary role in the community.

column5: less honorable parts receive greater honor
column6: Paul says the body's less honorable parts are treated with greater honor; this is a concrete reversal of rank within the community, not merely a claim that all parts exist.

column5: salvation as gift through faith
column6: The commentary says the final distinction is by faith and deeds; Ephesians says salvation comes by grace through faith as God's gift, locating its source in grace and faith rather than human achievement.

column5: works are not the basis for boasting
column6: Ephesians says salvation is not from works so that no one may boast, a specific difference from the commentary's formulation that righteous deeds help distinguish the saved.

column5: Arabic ء ن س and Hebrew אנוש; table correspondence, BDB notes Arabic cognate
column6: The commentary uses insan for the whole human species; Psalm 8 uses אנוש for the human being whom God remembers and crowns with glory and honor, a direct human-term correspondence with a strikingly dignified context.

column5: humanity crowned with glory and given dominion
column6: The commentary says all humanity is in loss regardless of rank; Psalm 8 depicts the human being as remembered, crowned with glory, and given dominion, adding a distinct account of dignity bestowed by God.

column5: Arabic خ س ر and Hebrew חסר; table sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary says high and low are included in khusr; at manna gathering, those who gather much have no surplus and those who gather little do not חסר, giving the table's unverified root match a specific scene of equal sufficiency.

column5: one father and Creator, shared obligation
column6: Malachi asks whether the community has one father and one Creator, then asks why its members betray one another; it connects common origin to ethical duty, while its immediate scope is covenant Israel rather than all humanity.

column5: all nations from one ancestor
column6: The commentary pairs lineage with the universal human category; Paul says God made every nation from one ancestor and appointed their times and boundaries, giving common human origin a concrete biblical formulation.

column5: all peoples directed to seek God
column6: Paul continues that the nations' situation is ordered so they might seek God; this adds a shared religious task to the common ancestry in the preceding verse.

column5: good works as the result of grace
column6: The preceding verses deny that works earn salvation, but Ephesians says believers are created in Christ for good works; this preserves a role for deeds while locating them as the result, not the basis, of salvation.

column5: Adam's seal and each person's uniqueness
column6: The Mishnah's single Adam is expanded: humanity bears one divine seal, yet no person resembles another and each must regard the world as created for them. This adds individual worth to the commentary's inclusion of every rank.

column5: Christian reception of Jeremiah's anti-boasting formula
column6: Clement applies Jeremiah's warning against boasting in wisdom, strength, and wealth to Christian humility, giving an early Christian interpretation of the status critique in Jeremiah 9.

column5: impartial correction and just judgment
column6: The church rule commands just judgment and no partiality when correcting transgressions; it gives the commentary's move from rank to religious conduct a concrete communal practice.

column5: associate with the lowly, do not be haughty
column6: Paul tells the community not to be proud and to associate with the lowly; the Greek can also mean associating with humble things, so this is a specific but textually ambiguous answer to elite distance from low-status people.
